mcq.q: A perfectly competitive firm sells 100 units at ₹40 each; its average total cost at that output is ₹35. Its supernormal profit is:
mcq.explain: Supernormal profit = (price − average total cost) × quantity = (40 − 35) × 100 = ₹500. Total revenue is ₹4,000 and total cost is ₹3,500; the difference is the supernormal profit. Normal profit is already included in average total cost in economics.
mcq.topic: Short run: supernormal profit, normal profit or loss

mcq.q: A perfectly competitive firm faces a market price of ₹18. At its best output, its average variable cost is ₹20 and average total cost ₹25. In the short run, the firm should:
options: Continue, because price covers average fixed cost
Continue, because losses are unavoidable anyway
Raise its price to ₹25
Shut down, because the price does not cover average variable cost
mcq.explain: In the short run a firm continues as long as price covers average variable cost, since it then recovers part of its fixed costs. Here price ₹18 is below AVC ₹20, so producing adds to the loss; the firm should shut down and lose only its fixed costs. A perfectly competitive firm cannot raise its own price.
mcq.topic: Short run: supernormal profit, normal profit or loss

mcq.q: Firms in a perfectly competitive industry are earning supernormal profits. In the long run:
options: New firms enter, industry supply rises and price falls until only normal profit remains
Supernormal profits continue forever
Existing firms leave the industry
The government fixes a higher price
mcq.explain: Perfect competition allows free entry. Supernormal profits attract new firms, which increase industry supply and push the market price down. Entry continues until price equals minimum long-run average cost and each firm earns only normal profit. Losses would work the other way, through exit.
mcq.topic: Long run: firm and industry under perfect competition
mcq.fast: Free entry wipes out supernormal profit in the long run.

mcq.q: A monopolist's average revenue is ₹50 at the profit-maximising output and price elasticity of demand there is 2. Its marginal revenue (and hence marginal cost) is:
mcq.explain: MR = AR × (1 − 1/e) = 50 × (1 − 1/2) = ₹25. Since a monopolist maximises profit where MR = MC, marginal cost at that output is also ₹25, while the price charged is ₹50. The gap between price and MC reflects the monopolist's market power.
mcq.fast: MR = AR (1 − 1/e); at equilibrium MC = MR.

mcq.q: A profit-maximising monopolist always operates on the part of its demand curve where demand is:
options: Inelastic (e less than 1)
Unit elastic
Elastic (e greater than 1)
Perfectly inelastic
mcq.explain: A monopolist produces where MR = MC. Marginal cost is positive, so MR must also be positive at equilibrium. Since MR = AR (1 − 1/e), MR is positive only when e > 1. Hence a monopolist never produces on the inelastic part of the demand curve.

mcq.q: Under price discrimination between two markets, a monopolist charges a higher price in the market where demand is:
options: Less elastic
More elastic
Perfectly elastic
Unit elastic
mcq.explain: A discriminating monopolist equates marginal revenue in each market with marginal cost. Since MR = P (1 − 1/e), equal MR means a higher price where elasticity is lower. Buyers who are less sensitive to price pay more, as with business travellers paying higher airfares than leisure travellers.

mcq.q: Which condition is necessary for price discrimination to be possible?
options: Elasticity of demand must be the same in all markets
The seller must face perfect competition
The markets must be separable, so goods cannot be resold from the cheap market to the dear market
The product must be homogeneous and freely resaleable
mcq.explain: Price discrimination requires that the seller has some monopoly power, that the markets can be kept separate so that buyers in the cheaper market cannot resell to those in the dearer market, and that the elasticities of demand differ between markets. If elasticities were equal, discrimination would not increase profit.
mcq.fast: Discrimination needs: monopoly power + separate markets + different elasticities.

mcq.q: In long-run equilibrium under monopolistic competition, a typical firm:
options: Earns supernormal profit
Produces at the minimum point of its LAC curve
Faces a horizontal demand curve
Earns only normal profit and operates with some excess capacity
mcq.explain: Free entry eliminates supernormal profits, so in the long run each firm earns normal profit with its downward-sloping demand curve tangent to the LAC curve. This tangency occurs to the left of the minimum point of LAC, so firms produce less than the optimum output — they have excess capacity.
mcq.fast: Monopolistic competition long run: normal profit + excess capacity.

mcq.q: The most distinctive feature of oligopoly is:
options: Interdependence of firms in taking price and output decisions
A single seller
Perfectly identical products and free entry
A large number of small firms
mcq.explain: In oligopoly a few firms dominate the market, so each firm's decisions affect the others and invite reactions. Every firm must consider how rivals will respond before changing its price or output. This mutual interdependence is the key feature that sets oligopoly apart from other market forms.

mcq.q: The kinked demand curve model of oligopoly (Sweezy) is used to explain:
options: How a monopolist discriminates prices
Why prices tend to remain rigid in oligopoly
Why firms earn normal profits in perfect competition
How cartels fix output quotas
mcq.explain: The kinked demand curve assumes that rivals will match a price cut but not a price rise. Demand is therefore elastic above the current price and inelastic below it, creating a kink and a gap in the MR curve. Changes in cost within that gap do not change the profit-maximising price, which explains price rigidity.

mcq.q: Which of the following is NOT a source of monopoly power?
options: Patents and copyrights
Control over an essential raw material
A large number of sellers offering identical products
Government licensing that allows only one producer
mcq.explain: Monopoly arises from barriers to entry — legal barriers such as patents, copyrights and exclusive licences; control of key raw materials; and natural monopoly where one firm can serve the whole market most cheaply. A large number of sellers of identical products describes perfect competition, the opposite of monopoly.
mcq.topic: Monopoly — features and how it arises
mcq.fast: Monopoly needs entry barriers; many sellers = competition.
